verdict.reasoning: Patient states being 'wheezy' and 'short of breath' for 'two, three days. Yeah, quite recently.'
Doctor asks about phlegm and patient replies 'No,' indicating a non-productive cough.
Patient says 'I have a fever' and later reports temperature 'thirty seven'; doctor asks 'Was it normal?' patient answers 'Yeah, yeah.' So subjective fever with measured 37°C is documented.
Patient reports being unable to walk to work due to feeling very short of breath: 'I also used to walk to work but recently I can't because... I feel like very short of breath.'
Patient states 'sometimes I feel like I can't even finish sentence... quite difficult to... complete the talking sometimes.'
When asked 'Any chest pain?' patient responds 'No chest pain, no.'
Patient says 'I used to walk to work but recently I... work from home or sometimes I take sick leave' and 'No, I can't' when asked about exercise, indicating exercise intolerance.
To 'are you... short of breath when you're sitting still? Or just when you walk?' patient answers 'Just walk... currently I feel well,' indicating comfort at rest.
Doctor asks about 'any... blood in there when you cough?' and patient replies 'No, I don't think so,' indicating no hemoptysis.

Patient had childhood asthma that was 'quite bad,' required inhalers, 'sometimes' hospital visits, but 'No, not that bad' regarding ICU, matching moderate–severe with intermittent hospital visits and no ICU.
Patient says 'I had asthma. I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema,' consistent with atopy including hay fever and eczema.

Patient states 'I took salbutamol... Normally, yeah' and uses it 'Every few weeks... What about when you exercise... do you have to use... inhalers? Patient: Yeah,' consistent with as-needed use every few weeks and sometimes before exercise.
On 'any allergies to medications?' patient replies 'No, no allergies,' indicating no known drug allergies.
Patient answers 'I live with my partner' and 'I'm engineer,' supporting living with partner and occupation as engineer.
To 'Do you smoke?' patient responds 'No, I don't smoke.'
Patient says 'one glass of wine' and 'Every two or three days? Depends, yeah,' matching about 1 glass every 2–3 days.
Patient states 'recently I, I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave,' due to breathing symptoms.

Doctor assesses 'it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma,' which by history with preserved rest function and no ICU/ER suggests mild to moderate exacerbation; this is a reasonable direct clinical inference.
Doctor says exacerbation 'could be, um, triggered by, if there's more pollen around, or... a viral infection,' matching likely triggers as viral infection or pollen/allergy.
Patient has hay fever and doctor recommends antihistamine; doctor links flare-up possibly to 'more pollen around,' indicating allergic rhinitis contributing to symptoms.
Patient explicitly states 'I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema.'

Doctor advises 'if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours? Initially,' and also prescribes a spacer to use inhaler more efficiently; together this is Salbutamol 2–4 puffs every 4 hours using a spacer.
Doctor: 'I can prescribe you... a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up.'
Doctor: 'I can prescribe you a peak flow meter... if you can record a value first thing when you wake up... And in the evening over the next week,' matching AM/PM values daily for 1 week.

Doctor only says 'if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway.' There is no mention of worsening exercise tolerance, trouble speaking, nocturnal symptoms, or lack of improvement as call-urgently criteria; those additions go beyond the transcript.

Doctor: 'it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review... You could arrange a review in a week or so... we may need to start some other medication for you' and later 'see whether you need to go on another inhaler as well,' consistent with asthma review in ~1 week to consider controller based on symptoms/peak flow.

Doctor: 'the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy, I can put a on your notes about what to take.' This matches starting daily OTC antihistamines with pharmacist guidance.
There is no advice in the transcript about gradually returning to activity or avoiding triggers; this is new guidance not mentioned.

Doctor advises arranging 'a review in a week or so' and also 'then we can discuss that over the phone when we look at the figures,' and earlier says to 'call us back straightaway' if worsening, matching a phone review in 1 week with peak flow log and earlier contact if symptoms deteriorate.
